purpose: Structured, interconnected dog training and behaviour knowledge library for a reward-based, welfare-centred mobile app.
copyright_note: Original synthesis. Woofz is used only as topic and user-experience inspiration. No Woofz wording, videos, graphics or proprietary lesson sequences are reproduced.
progression_note: The 80/60/40 success rule is an app design heuristic, not a universal scientific threshold.

lessons.title: Choose reinforcement
lessons.objective: Teach and practise choose reinforcement as a voluntary, reward-based skill.
lessons.why_it_matters: Builds a useful behaviour while supporting clear communication, welfare and reliable real-world performance.
lessons.setup: Use a quiet, safe environment with the dog comfortable and able to engage.
lessons.steps: Set up the easiest version of the exercise. | Wait for or prompt the target behaviour. | Mark the correct moment. | Deliver the reward promptly. | Repeat for a few short repetitions. | End while the dog is still successful and comfortable.
lessons.success_criteria: At least 4 successful repetitions out of 5 in the current setup, without signs of distress or excessive arousal.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.
lessons.professional_help_if: Behaviour is worsening, the dog appears distressed, or progress repeatedly stalls despite appropriate regression and management.
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release

lessons.why_it_matters: Builds a useful behaviour while supporting clear communication, welfare and reliable real-world performance.
lessons.setup: Use a quiet, safe environment with the dog comfortable and able to engage.
lessons.steps: Set up the easiest version of the exercise. | Wait for or prompt the target behaviour. | Mark the correct moment. | Deliver the reward promptly. | Repeat for a few short repetitions. | End while the dog is still successful and comfortable.
lessons.success_criteria: At least 4 successful repetitions out of 5 in the current setup, without signs of distress or excessive arousal.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.
lessons.professional_help_if: Behaviour is worsening, the dog appears distressed, or progress repeatedly stalls despite appropriate regression and management.
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release

behaviours.name: Jumping up
behaviours.possible_functions: Greeting reinforcement, excitement, attention, learned habit
behaviours.management: Prevent rehearsal where practical; create space; reinforce four paws on floor or another compatible behaviour.
behaviours.training_route: LIFE greeting lessons → CALM regulation → COM focus → generalisation

behaviours.name: Pulling on lead
behaviours.possible_functions: Access to environment, movement, social contact, scent, frustration or excitement
behaviours.management: Use suitable equipment, create distance from triggers and avoid rehearsing intense pulling.
behaviours.training_route: COM check-in → WAL loose lead → WAL this way → CALM → REACT if trigger-related

behaviours.name: Barking
behaviours.possible_functions: Alerting, fear, frustration, attention, arousal, access or habit
behaviours.management: Identify triggers and reduce unnecessary rehearsal; provide distance and alternative behaviours.
behaviours.training_route: ASSESS barking record → BARK decision tree → CALM/COM → trigger-specific work

behaviours.name: Growling
behaviours.possible_functions: Distance-increasing communication, discomfort, guarding, fear or conflict
behaviours.management: Do not punish the warning; increase safety and investigate context and possible pain.
behaviours.training_route: SAFE → ASSESS → medical screen → behaviour modification

behaviours.name: Biting
behaviours.management: Immediate safety, separation and appropriate professional/veterinary support.
behaviours.training_route: SAFE biting decision tree → professional assessment

behaviours.name: Resource guarding
behaviours.possible_functions: Protection of valued resource, learned history, fear of loss
behaviours.management: Avoid confrontation and forced removal; manage access and teach trades where safe.
behaviours.training_route: RG management → trade → gradual approach-and-add work where appropriate → referral if severe

behaviours.name: Destruction
behaviours.possible_functions: Chewing, exploration, frustration, boredom, access, separation distress
behaviours.management: Dog-proof area, provide legal chew/enrichment and identify whether destruction occurs when alone.
behaviours.training_route: CHEW assessment → enrichment → home management → ALONE pathway if alone-related

behaviours.name: Toileting indoors
behaviours.possible_functions: Incomplete training, access, schedule, marking, fear or medical issue
behaviours.management: Increase access to appropriate toilet area and reward immediately; clean accidents thoroughly; avoid punishment.
behaviours.training_route: HOME toilet routine → ASSESS medical/environment screen

behaviours.name: Chasing
behaviours.possible_functions: Predatory sequence, play, excitement, movement sensitivity
behaviours.management: Prevent access to dangerous situations; use secure equipment and distance.
behaviours.training_route: CHASE management → COM check-in → this-way → long-line skills

behaviours.name: Reactivity
behaviours.possible_functions: Fear, frustration, excitement, conflict or overwhelm
behaviours.management: Distance, trigger avoidance where needed, predictable escape routes, reduce trigger stacking.
behaviours.training_route: REACT assessment → threshold → disengagement → counter-conditioning → generalisation

behaviours.name: Separation distress
behaviours.management: Avoid prolonged panic; use gradual absence work and professional support for significant distress.
behaviours.training_route: ALONE baseline → gradual independence → referral when severe

protocols.name: Reward-based skill acquisition
protocols.route: Set up easy → prompt/capture → marker → reward → repeat → fade prompt → add cue → generalise
protocols.success: Stable success without distress; app heuristic: ≥80% current-stage success before progression.

protocols.name: Behaviour change core loop
protocols.route: Observe → safety/health screen → manage → identify likely function/emotional state → teach alternative → reinforce → generalise → measure
protocols.success: Trend improves in frequency, intensity, duration, distance or recovery.

protocols.name: Threshold-based trigger work
protocols.route: Find workable distance → pair trigger with reinforcement → allow disengagement → gradually alter distance/context → regress if stress rises
protocols.success: Dog can notice trigger and remain able to learn/recover.

protocols.name: Trade protocol
protocols.trigger: Dog has an item that should be released
protocols.route: Start with low-value item → present better reward → dog releases → mark/reward → return item when safe → gradually increase value
protocols.success: Voluntary release with relaxed body language.

protocols.name: Recall protocol
protocols.route: Cue once → encourage if needed → mark commitment/arrival → high-value reward → often release back to activity
protocols.success: Prompt return in current environment without needing repeated cues.

protocols.name: Alone-time protocol
protocols.route: Establish baseline → very short absence → return before distress → increase gradually → regress after reaction
protocols.success: Dog remains comfortable at current absence duration.

protocols.name: Professional handoff
protocols.route: Create structured history → trigger map → frequency/intensity/duration → safety incidents → management → training history → referral

safety_gates.name: Immediate danger / bite injury
safety_gates.trigger: Immediate risk to a person or animal, serious bite, uncontrolled aggression or emergency.
safety_gates.action: Stop training, create safe separation and seek urgent veterinary/medical or emergency support as appropriate.

safety_gates.name: Aggression toward people with bite history
safety_gates.trigger: Dog has bitten or repeatedly attempted to bite a person.
safety_gates.action: Do not run DIY exposure exercises; use secure management and arrange qualified behaviour support.

safety_gates.name: Sudden behaviour change / possible pain
safety_gates.trigger: New or abruptly worsened behaviour, especially handling sensitivity, aggression, withdrawal or altered movement.
safety_gates.action: Arrange veterinary assessment before assuming the issue is purely training.

safety_gates.name: Severe resource guarding
safety_gates.trigger: Guarding includes bites, repeated attacks, guarding people, dangerous objects or escalating intensity.
safety_gates.action: Manage access safely and seek qualified behaviour support; avoid confrontation or forcibly taking items.

safety_gates.name: Severe separation distress
safety_gates.trigger: Panic, escape attempts, self-injury or severe distress when alone.
safety_gates.action: Avoid prolonged distress and seek veterinary/qualified behaviour support.

safety_gates.name: Severe fear / panic
safety_gates.trigger: Dog is unable to eat, learn or recover because of intense fear/panic.
safety_gates.action: Increase distance/remove pressure and seek professional guidance if persistent or severe.

safety_gates.name: Traffic / escape risk
safety_gates.trigger: Repeated lunging toward traffic or wildlife creates a realistic risk of escape or injury.
safety_gates.action: Prioritise secure equipment and management; do not test recall near hazards.

safety_gates.name: Child / dog interaction risk
safety_gates.trigger: Dog shows fear, guarding, snapping, chasing or unpredictable behaviour around children.
safety_gates.action: Use active separation/management and obtain professional guidance; never rely on a child's ability to read the dog.

safety_gates.name: Dog cannot be safely handled
safety_gates.trigger: Dog cannot safely tolerate routine handling or equipment application.
safety_gates.action: Do not force handling; seek veterinary and/or cooperative-care behaviour support.

safety_gates.name: Possible medical / neurological issue
safety_gates.trigger: Collapse, seizure-like episodes, disorientation, unusual movement, acute pain or major cognitive change.

safety_gates.name: Professional referral threshold
safety_gates.trigger: Repeated failure despite appropriate training, complex behaviour, significant welfare impact or household safety concern.
safety_gates.action: Refer to an appropriately qualified reward-based professional; consider veterinary input.

safety_gates.name: Muzzle / management referral
safety_gates.trigger: A muzzle may be needed to reduce risk during unavoidable situations.
safety_gates.action: Use humane conditioning and appropriate equipment; seek professional advice where bite risk is significant.

evidence_sources.title: Positive reinforcement training with rewards
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reward-based training can use food, toys, attention and environmental rewards; reward new behaviours clearly and consistently.
evidence_sources.limitations: Practical guidance rather than a systematic review.

evidence_sources.title: Introducing a marker
evidence_sources.key_finding: A marker precisely identifies the desired behaviour and is followed immediately by reinforcement.

evidence_sources.title: Focus training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Attention and voluntary check-ins are foundational skills; practise in easy environments before adding distraction.

evidence_sources.title: Name training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Pair the dog's name with looking toward the handler and reinforcement; avoid repeatedly saying the name without consequence.

evidence_sources.title: Sit training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Lure or shape the behaviour, mark the correct moment and fade the lure; do not physically push the dog into position.

evidence_sources.title: Down training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Lure or shape a down and reinforce it; avoid forcing the dog into position.

evidence_sources.title: Stay training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Build duration before adding distance and distraction; reward while the dog remains in position and generalise gradually.

evidence_sources.title: Settle training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reinforce relaxed behaviour and gradually increase duration and distraction.

evidence_sources.title: Leave training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Teach the dog that moving away from an item leads to reinforcement; increase item value and distraction gradually.

evidence_sources.title: Recall training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Build a highly reinforced recall from easy settings, then add distance and distraction; use a long line and harness where appropriate.

evidence_sources.title: Target training
evidence_sources.key_finding: A hand target can provide a clear behaviour for focus and redirection; regress if the dog becomes confused or frustrated.

evidence_sources.title: Reactive dog
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reactivity may reflect worry, frustration, excitement or overwhelm; distance, management and gradual behaviour change are important.
evidence_sources.limitations: Not a substitute for an individual behaviour assessment.

evidence_sources.title: Dog training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reward-based training, short regular sessions and gradual reduction of distractions are recommended.

evidence_sources.title: Dog behaviour
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reward desirable behaviour, avoid shouting/punishment and seek veterinary or behaviour support for serious problems or behaviour change.

evidence_sources.title: Loose-lead walking
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reward attention and a loose lead; stop or change direction when pulling makes progress impossible.

evidence_sources.title: Toilet training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Watch for signs, take the dog to the correct place and reward promptly; avoid punishment for accidents.

evidence_sources.title: Left alone
evidence_sources.key_finding: Increase alone time gradually and return to an easier stage if the dog reacts.
evidence_sources.limitations: Individual separation cases may need professional support.

evidence_sources.title: Trainer guidance
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reward-based methods should be used; fear, pain, choking, shouting and hitting should be avoided.

evidence_sources.title: Dog and puppy training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Positive reward-based training, short sessions and practice in different locations are recommended.

evidence_sources.title: Recall training
evidence_sources.key_finding: Make recall valuable, practise in easy settings, use a long line and harness outdoors when needed, and do not punish returns.

evidence_sources.title: Stop pulling on the lead
evidence_sources.key_finding: Reward loose lead and calmness; stop when pulling; progress gradually.

evidence_sources.title: Recall
evidence_sources.key_finding: Build recall positively with valuable rewards, secure practice and gradual increases in distraction.

evidence_sources.title: Walk on lead
evidence_sources.key_finding: Start calm, reinforce loose-lead movement and separate structured walking from sniff/exploration opportunities.

evidence_sources.title: This way
evidence_sources.key_finding: A trained direction-change cue can help create space from distractions and support loose-lead walking.

evidence_sources.title: ABTC owner and practitioner guidance
evidence_sources.key_finding: UK animal training and behaviour roles should be science-led, compassionate and welfare-centred; practitioner roles differ by complexity.
evidence_sources.limitations: Professional standard rather than treatment guideline.

evidence_sources.title: Animal Training Instructor Standard
evidence_sources.key_finding: Training should be tailored to life stage, health, learning principles, history and temperament, with evaluation and welfare safeguards.
evidence_sources.limitations: Defines professional competency rather than a single training protocol.

evidence_sources.title: Humane Dog Training Position Statement
evidence_sources.key_finding: AVSAB recommends reward-based methods for canine training and behaviour modification and advises against aversive methods.
evidence_sources.limitations: Position statement synthesising available evidence and professional consensus.

evidence_sources.title: Reward-based training methods
evidence_sources.key_finding: Explains reinforcement and punishment terminology and welfare risks associated with aversive approaches.

evidence_sources.title: Woofz overview
evidence_sources.key_finding: Woofz demonstrates a consumer app structure involving personalised plans, commands, programmes, games and troubleshooting.
evidence_sources.limitations: Commercial product; not treated as evidence authority.

evidence_sources.title: Ultimate dog training guide
evidence_sources.key_finding: Useful as topic/UX inspiration only.
evidence_sources.limitations: Not used as sole authority; no wording, graphics, videos or proprietary sequences reproduced.

evidence_cards.summary: Strong welfare and professional support for reward-based approaches.
evidence_cards.does_not_mean: Rewards alone guarantee a result or remove the need for management.

evidence_cards.summary: Major professional bodies advise against aversive methods because of welfare and behaviour risks.
evidence_cards.does_not_mean: The app should ignore safety; management and professional support remain essential.

evidence_cards.summary: Operational app concept: the point where a dog becomes unable to respond or learn effectively around a trigger.
evidence_cards.does_not_mean: A single fixed distance applies to all dogs or all days.

evidence_cards.summary: Multiple stressors or arousing events may affect subsequent behaviour and recovery.
evidence_cards.does_not_mean: There is a universal recovery duration that applies to every dog.

evidence_cards.summary: App design heuristic for progression decisions.
evidence_cards.does_not_mean: It is a validated universal threshold or a measure of dog quality.

evidence_cards.summary: Low-risk trades can be taught, but severe guarding or bite risk requires management and professional support.
evidence_cards.does_not_mean: Every guarding case is suitable for DIY behaviour modification.

progression_rules.name: App success heuristic
progression_rules.note: Design heuristic, not a universal scientific threshold.

progression_rules.name: One-variable progression
progression_rules.action: Increase one major difficulty dimension at a time.
progression_rules.note: Dimensions: duration, distance, distraction, environment, arousal, competing reward, handler difficulty.

progression_rules.name: Stress override
progression_rules.condition: Stress/arousal rises sharply or dog stops being able to learn
progression_rules.action: Regress immediately or end session; safety and welfare override performance goals.
progression_rules.note: Do not chase a percentage target when welfare is deteriorating.

progression_rules.name: Generalisation
progression_rules.condition: Skill is reliable in one context
progression_rules.action: Change people, places, surfaces, distractions or time gradually.
progression_rules.note: Reliability in one context does not imply generalisation.

progression_rules.name: Recovery trend
progression_rules.action: Record recovery time and adjust future difficulty based on trend.
progression_rules.note: Recovery is a useful measure alongside frequency and intensity.

myths.myth: Dogs need to be shown who is boss.
myths.reality: Dominance-based explanations are not a sound default for everyday training; focus on learning history, environment, emotions, reinforcement and safety.

myths.myth: If you reward growling you teach aggression.
myths.reality: Punishing warning signals can remove communication without resolving the underlying problem. Treat growling as information and assess context/safety.

myths.myth: The dog knows what I asked but is deliberately ignoring me.
myths.reality: Performance depends on context, reinforcement history, distraction, arousal, health and whether the behaviour has been generalised.

myths.myth: A tired dog is a trained dog.
myths.reality: Exercise can meet needs, but fatigue is not a substitute for teaching skills or addressing emotional/behavioural causes.

myths.myth: Dogs must greet lots of other dogs.
myths.reality: Safe neutrality and the ability to disengage are valuable outcomes; social exposure should be individualised and consent-aware.

myths.myth: Just keep repeating the exercise until the dog gets it.
myths.reality: Repeated failure usually means the setup needs changing: lower distraction, shorten duration, increase reward value or teach a prerequisite.
Food can be reinforcement; prompts can be faded and reinforcement schedules can vary once behaviour is established.

myths.myth: You should never use treats after a behaviour is learned.
myths.reality: Reinforcement remains useful; its frequency and type can change while maintaining behaviour.

daily_programmes.name: 10-minute foundation
daily_programmes.route: FND marker → COM name/check-in → SKL sit/down → CALM settle

daily_programmes.name: 10-minute walking prep
daily_programmes.route: COM check-in → WAL this-way → loose-lead repetitions → sniff reward
daily_programmes.feedback: Regress if lead tension becomes persistent.

daily_programmes.name: 10-minute recall
daily_programmes.route: Indoor recall → recall away from toy → recall and release → garden/long-line if ready
daily_programmes.feedback: Never test unreliable recall near hazards.

daily_programmes.name: 10-minute calmness
daily_programmes.route: Capture calm → mat → short settle → mild movement → reward recovery
daily_programmes.feedback: Use easier distractions if arousal rises.

daily_programmes.name: 10-minute enrichment
daily_programmes.route: Find-it → sniff search → simple shaping → approved chew
daily_programmes.feedback: Choose activities that match the dog's preferences and welfare.

daily_programmes.name: 10-minute real-world generalisation
daily_programmes.route: Known skill → new location → low distraction → reward → short recovery period
daily_programmes.feedback: Change one context variable at a time.

owner_guidance.guidance: Prefer short, successful sessions. End before frustration or fatigue becomes the dominant feature.
Use rewards the dog genuinely values. Food, play, attention and access to preferred activities can all function as reinforcement.
The database is built around reward-based training and does not recommend pain, fear or intimidation as training tools.
Management is not failure. Preventing rehearsal creates safer conditions in which new behaviour can be learned.
A sudden behaviour change, pain signs or unusual neurological signs warrant veterinary assessment rather than assuming a training problem.
For serious aggression, bite history, severe guarding, panic or complex behaviour, use an appropriately qualified professional and consider veterinary involvement.

success_heuristic.note: Heuristic only; welfare and emotional state override performance percentages.
